extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science and educated general readers interested in American public opinion (early 20th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying the organs, national characteristics, and practical signs by which public opinion in the United States is formed and read (as discussed in an early‑20th‑century political science text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Press tendency: news rather than views
rubrics_metrics.description: American journals 'lay themselves out to give news rather than views' and are less bound to a particular party than many European papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes the American press less powerful in shaping opinion than some Old World papers, but bolder papers can aid reform by exposing corruption. Beware that press writing often reflects what writers wish to be believed rather than what people actually think; local papers may at times be influenced by potent local forces and fail to say what ought to be said.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personal conversation to test public sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A politician travelling abroad will 'lose touch' of current sentiment and needs 'an hour's talk with four or five discerning friends' of different types to gather how facts strike the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudent observers keep a circle of such friends to test and correct impressions — conversation with judicious non‑political observers often yields things the press will not. This is an explicit corrective to relying solely on newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and form of public meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: In America meetings are usually held for practical objects (selection of candidates, organization) rather than as mere demonstrations of opinion or instruction; political lectures are often paid engagements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meetings outside campaigns tend toward organization and enthusiasm rather than argumentative speaking; during campaigns attendees are assumed to be of one party and meetings supply fervor more than persuasion. In England, meetings are more used to elicit and cultivate opinion — a contrast to note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elections and polls as the sure index of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The polls are the only sure index of opinion' so every election — even small ones — is watched closely and compared with previous votes to infer trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State contests immediately before presidential elections are especially scrutinized. Caution: too much weight is often attributed to small or local contests (by‑elections), which may be influenced by purely local causes; such contests can nevertheless indicate displeasure and prompt party course‑corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associations and voluntary organizations as opinion organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Associations (temperance societies, campaign clubs, local committees) are created and worked quickly in the U.S. and act as organs for focusing and propagating opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They rouse attention, excite discussion, formulate principles, embolden members, and create impressions of a spreading movement that draws recruits. Observing attendance, language, zeal, and organization reveals which ideas are taking hold. Money for such organizations is plentiful and rapidly subscribed for political purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban versus rural formation of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Urban life produces certain formative influences (political leaders, testing of ideas in conversation) that are stronger in densely populated countries; in the U.S. these urban influences tell somewhat less because a smaller proportion of the population live in large cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a large share of Americans are rural, city‑based methods of opinion formation and diffusion have less overall weight; nevertheless reading habits and social instincts mitigate this difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: National social homogeneity aids reading opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Social distinctions count for less in America' so tendencies are more uniformly diffused through classes, making it easier for an observer to gather national tendencies than in more stratified societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Easier social intercourse and fewer people unaffiliated with parties reduce unpredictable votes; yet discerning changes and predicting consequences remains difficult and observers may still err.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty and uncertainty in discerning true opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion's organs often 'give an uncertain sound' — many small local changes and 'wavelets' can mislead an observer about the main stream of opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interposition of party 'Machine' elements can act as non‑conductors between public opinion and legislators. Observers must watch many minor variations before concluding a real movement; mistakes usually stem from personal bias or vanity rather than lack of materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders should follow rather than force opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: American leaders generally 'take the course which they believe the people at the moment desire' rather than seeking to anticipate or force opinion; a statesman who courageously tells people they are wrong may be respected if he refuses to be their instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders risk provoking reaction if they force opinion. Mistaking eddies and cross‑currents for the main stream often leads to political failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: National character: good‑natured, kindly disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Native Americans are described as a good‑natured, kindly people disposed to charitable views of others; anger fades quickly and cruelty is abhorred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This temperament influences civic behavior — juries are more lenient (except in offences against women), former rebels were quickly forgiven after the Civil War, and vindictiveness in public men provokes disapproval; a tendency to let bygones be bygones can sometimes let misdeeds be forgotten when they should not be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pervasive sense of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: A distributed national sense of the ludicrous — Americans are 'conspicuously the purveyors of humour' — colors ordinary life and conversation and helps leaders (e.g., Lincoln) restore confidence by a humorous turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour shapes public discourse and can reduce bitterness; it also fosters an indulgent view of mankind and may produce an appearance of lack of seriousness with political implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hopefulness and optimism
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans are a hopeful people ('feel in their veins the bounding pulse of youth') who look to a long future to remedy faults and exploit vast resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sanguine temper makes them tolerant of evils seen as transitory and fosters confidence in progress; it colors receptivity to reforms and patience with gradual change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unbounded faith in the People and democratic system
rubrics_metrics.description: There is strong faith that majority rule will, in the long run, decide rightly; truth and justice are expected to make their way into majority minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This axiom leads many to trust popular sovereignty and to view minorities who are right as likely to win converts over time. A related idea is that majority status proves right — an attitude with political and moral consequences to be examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: High average education but often superficial
rubrics_metrics.description: Native Americans are relatively well educated (knowledge of the Constitution, habit of reading) but that education is often superficial — sufficient to think they know about politics but insufficient to grasp how little they know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common schools provide the key skills (reading/writing) and civic basics but do not teach citizens how to use them for deep judgment; hence voters may be ill‑fitted to weigh statesmen's merits or complex issues despite feeling capable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and religious character; reforming zeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The people are broadly moral, well‑conducted, and (especially native stock in Eastern and Middle States) religious — pious without superstition, zealous without bigotry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religion influences conduct and fuels numerous philanthropic and reformatory agencies; zeal often outruns discretion, producing over‑ambitious legislative or voluntary attempts to suppress vice or 'purify' literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreverential practical independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans are 'unreverential' in that they are little disposed to defer to the opinions of those wiser or better instructed in public questions; politics is seen as within every practical man's comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lowers deference to special knowledge in politics, makes oratory aimed at stimulation rather than instruction, and produces a political culture where practical competence in running elections is valued over studied statesmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local government experience lowers expected national standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Because local government is highly popular and complete, citizens judge national politics by what they know locally and expect the same standards to suffice for national office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrows the perceived gap between municipal competence and national statesmanship, discourages leaders from adopting high, instructive tones (fear of ridicule), and makes ridicule a powerful political weapon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Busyness and lack of leisure for political thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The citizen has little time for sustained political thought because business and other pursuits occupy most hours; political interest peaks in presidential years and campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At most times political questions fall into the background, especially among commercial and urban classes; village life and local government sustain more continuous interest. This temporal unevenness affects the depth and steadiness of public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aversion to steady, patient thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans' quick perceptions and emphasis on action lead to a tendency to ignore difficulties and evade them rather than conduct minute investigation and patient reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trait helps business success but preserves certain prejudices and fallacies in social and economic thought; the pressure of practical life often prevents finding the time needed for deep analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial, profit‑oriented outlook
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans commonly apply practical, profit‑and‑loss tests to men and measures, assuming successful people are 'smart' and schemes that 'pay well' deserve support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract or subtle reasoning is distrusted; the public prefers plain, apprehensible arguments. While open to listening, Americans can be hard to convince because they believe they have already thought through most issues in line with local or party prevailing notions.
